traps: Not factorising first, so cubic numerators and denominators appear and nothing can be cancelled (Summer 2018 Q8)

noteBlocks.text: Why cancelling works, and when it does not

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing at the top, whatever multiplies both lines is struck from both. What is left is the answer, and every FM1 algebraic fraction question needs this move.

Cancelling is division: it divides the top and the bottom by the same thing, leaving the value alone. So only a **factor** can go, something the whole line is multiplied by. A **term** is added to the rest of its line; dividing it alone does not divide the line.

In $\frac{x(x+8)}{5x}$ the $x$ multiplies the whole top, so it divides out: $\frac{x(x+8)}{5x}=\frac{x+8}{5}$. In $\frac{x+8}{5x}$ it is a term: at $x=2$ that fraction is $1$, but striking the $x$ leaves $\frac{8}{5}$, so it stays.

noteBlocks.explain: Only something that multiplies a whole line can be struck from it. The $x$ on top is added to the $4$, so it is a term, and there is no $4$ underneath to match. Test it as the worked lines did: at $x=1$ the fraction is $5$, while $4$ is $4$. So nothing cancels.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, the square $x^{2}$ loses the corner $a^{2}$, and the strip that moves round turns what is left into a rectangle $x+a$ long and $x-a$ wide. So a square minus a square always splits into two brackets, one plus and one minus: $x^{2}-a^{2}=(x+a)(x-a)$.
So $x^{2}-49=(x+7)(x-7)$, because $49=7^{2}$. Multiply back to check: $x^{2}-7x+7x-49$, and the two middle terms cancel. That is why this shape never has an $x$ term.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $x^{2}-9$ as a product of two brackets?
noteBlocks.explain: Nine is $3^{2}$, so $x^{2}-9$ is a square minus a square: one bracket takes $+3$, the other $-3$, and the middle terms cancel when you multiply back. $(x+3)^{2}$ gives $x^{2}+6x+9$, and $(x+9)(x-1)$ gives $x^{2}+8x-9$. So it is $(x+3)(x-3)$.

noteBlocks.text: Two squares with a number in front

noteBlocks.md: When the $x^{2}$ carries a square number, split it the same way, taking the square root of each part. The root of $16x^{2}$ is $4x$, not $16x$, because $4x$ times $4x$ is $16x^{2}$. Summer 2022 examiners often saw $4x^{2}-1$ left unfactorised, so look for this shape.

noteBlocks.explain: Take the square root of each part, as the worked lines did: $36x^{2}=(6x)^{2}$ and $25=5^{2}$, so the brackets hold $6x$ and $5$, one plus and one minus. $(36x+5)(36x-5)$ would start $1296x^{2}$, and $(6x+5)^{2}$ has a middle term, $60x$. So it is $(6x+5)(6x-5)$.

noteBlocks.md: Before any brackets, look for what every term shares: a number, an $x$, or both. In the drawing both pieces are $3x$ tall, so $3x^{2}+30x=3x(x+10)$. Taking the common factor out first often uncovers two squares.
$3x^{2}-300$ looks stuck until the 3 comes out: $3x^{2}-300=3(x^{2}-100)$, which becomes $3(x+10)(x-10)$. Keep the 3 in the answer: it is a factor, not something to divide away.

noteBlocks.title: Beyond this specification
noteBlocks.md: The statement names linear and quadratic numerators and denominators, and no FM1 paper from 2018 to 2026 sets a cubic. If one ever appears, the first move is the same: $x^{3}-100x=x(x^{2}-100)$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A numerator is $x^{3}-9x$. What is the first line you write?
options: It is a cubic, so it does not factorise
noteBlocks.explain: Look for what every term shares first: both terms carry an $x$, so it comes out, giving $x(x^{2}-9)$, and the bracket is then two squares, $x(x+3)(x-3)$. Writing $(x-3)(x+3)$ drops the $x$: multiplied out it is $x^{2}-9$, not $x^{3}-9x$. So the first line is $x(x^{2}-9)$.

noteBlocks.md: Every simplification is the same three moves. First, factorise the top fully, common factor first. Second, factorise the bottom the same way. Third, strike every factor both lines share, numbers included, and check that nothing else divides both.

Take $\frac{2x^{2}-128}{x^{2}+17x+72}$. Top: $2x^{2}-128=2(x+8)(x-8)$. Bottom: $x^{2}+17x+72=(x+8)(x+9)$, since $8\times9=72$ and $8+9=17$. Strike $(x+8)$ from both lines, and the answer is $\frac{2(x-8)}{x+9}$.

noteBlocks.title: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions
noteBlocks.why: The whole method at writing speed, on several shapes the paper uses. Watch it once, then answer the next check without going back.

noteBlocks.explain: Factorise first, as the worked lines did: the top is $(x+7)(x+2)$ and the bottom is $(x+7)(x-2)$, so $(x+7)$ divides out. Striking the two $x^{2}$ terms instead cancels terms of a sum, and stopping at the factorised line leaves $(x+7)$ on both lines. The answer is $\frac{x+2}{x-2}$.

noteBlocks.md: The instruction is **simplify fully**, and the last mark goes on that word. Fully means nothing at all still divides both lines: no bracket, no number and no lone $x$. So when the brackets are gone, look at the numbers and at any $x$ left.
In $\frac{8}{4(x-7)}$ the 8 and the 4 share a 4, so $\frac{8}{4(x-7)}=\frac{2}{x-7}$. Multiplying the bracket out instead gives $\frac{8}{4x-28}$, which only hides that factor.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024, FM1 Q8(a)
noteBlocks.md: Most candidates factorised every expression and cancelled correctly, and then a high number stopped one step early, leaving a factor of 2 in the answer. The algebra was right, and the final mark was lost.

noteBlocks.explain: Look at the numbers, as the worked lines did: the 14 and the 7 share a factor of 7, so dividing both by 7 gives $\frac{2}{x-9}$. Multiplying the bracket out to $\frac{14}{7x-63}$ only hides that factor. So no: it becomes $\frac{2}{x-9}$.

noteBlocks.title: Why a lone number or x still counts
noteBlocks.md: A 2 over a 4, or an $x$ over an $x$, divides the whole top and the whole bottom just as a bracket does, so it is a common factor too. An answer is fully simplified only when nothing divides both lines.
So $\frac{5x^{2}}{x}$ is not finished: $x$ divides both lines, and $\frac{5x^{2}}{x}=5x$. In the same way, $\frac{12x}{3x}=4$, a whole number.

noteBlocks.prompt: Sam has reached $\frac{6x^{2}}{x}$. Is that the answer?
options: No — an $x$ divides both lines, giving $6x$
noteBlocks.answer: No — an $x$ divides both lines, giving $6x$
noteBlocks.explain: Look for a lone $x$, as the worked lines did: $6x^{2}$ is $6x$ times $x$, and the bottom is $x$, so $x$ divides both lines and leaves $6x$. Striking only the $x$ underneath, to get $6x^{2}$, changes the value. So no: it becomes $6x$.

noteBlocks.md: **It ends a division.** Most often the fraction comes out of a division (2021 to 2025). Multiply by the second fraction turned over, so $\div\frac{x+9}{2}$ becomes $\times\frac{2}{x+9}$; then factorise every line, so $x^{2}+9x$ becomes $x(x+9)$.
**'Simplest form' means fully.** When a question asks for one fraction in its simplest form (2018, 2022), it wants exactly what **simplify fully** wants: nothing left that divides both lines.

**'Hence' hands you the top.** One part may ask you to expand, and the next to simplify fully using it (2019). Collect the new numerator, then factorise it and keep the number you take out: $3x^{2}+24x=3x(x+8)$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Part (i) built the numerator $2x^{2}+14x$. Part (ii) says simplify fully. What is your first line for that numerator?
noteBlocks.explain: Factorise the line you were given and keep what comes out: both terms share $2x$, so the top is $2x(x+7)$. Dividing the line by 2 gives $x^{2}+7x$, a different expression, as Summer 2019 examiners saw; leaving it as it is hides every factor. So the first line is $2x(x+7)$.

noteBlocks.md:
Factorise both lines fully: common factor first, then two squares or a quadratic.
Cancel only factors, never terms; test with a number if unsure.
Finish on the numbers and any lone $x$: nothing may divide both lines.
Treat 'simplest form', 'hence' and a division as the same job.

On FM1 this move rarely stands alone: **simplify fully**, or one fraction in its simplest form, usually finishes a division, addition or subtraction worth 4 to 7 marks, between Q7 and Q12 (2018 to 2026). Schemes give MW1 marks for factorising, M1 for turning a division into a multiplication, and the last mark for the fully simplified answer. So factorise every line first, even before you see where it leads.

items.skill: Tell a factor from a term

options.feedback: The $x$ on top is added to the $11$, so it is a term, not a factor of the whole top. At $x=2$ the fraction is $\frac{13}{4}$, but striking the $x$ gives $\frac{11}{2}$.
The whole top is $x$ times $(x+11)$, so $x$ is a factor of both lines and divides out, leaving $\frac{x+11}{2}$.
The $x$ divides the $x^{2}$ but not the $11$, so it is not a factor of the whole top. At $x=2$ the fraction is $\frac{15}{4}$, but striking an $x$ gives $\frac{13}{2}$.

items.stem: What is the first move when you simplify $\frac{x^{2}+11x+30}{x^{2}+x-30}$?

options.text: Factorise the top and the bottom
options.feedback: Always. Until both lines are products, there is nothing that can legitimately be cancelled.

options.text: Cancel the $x^{2}$ on the top with the $x^{2}$ on the bottom
options.feedback: Those are terms of a sum, so they cannot be cancelled. Factorise first: the top is $(x+5)(x+6)$ and the bottom $(x+6)(x-5)$, and then $(x+6)$ may go.

options.text: Divide every term on both lines by $x$
options.feedback: Dividing through by $x$ leaves fractions inside the expression and hides the factors. Factorise first and the common bracket appears on its own.

items.skill: Recognise a difference of two squares with a coefficient

options.feedback: $9x^{2}-25$ is $9x^{2}$ minus $25$, so it is $(3x)^{2}-5^{2}$ and the two brackets are $(3x-5)$ and $(3x+5)$.
Multiply that out and the $x^{2}$ term is $81x^{2}$. The square root of $9x^{2}$ is $3x$, not $9x$.
That is $9x^{2}-30x+25$, which has a middle term. A difference of two squares has no middle term because the two cross terms cancel.

items.stem: Kara has reached $\frac{6}{3(x-3)}$ when simplifying $\frac{6x+18}{3x^{2}-27}$. What still has to happen?

options.feedback: The brackets are done and the numbers are not. The last mark on these questions is almost always for the number.

options.text: Nothing more — it is already fully simplified
options.feedback: The 6 and the 3 share a factor of 3. Summer 2024 examiners reported a high number of candidates stopping exactly here.
Multiplying out hides the factors and does not simplify anything. The bracket form is what lets you see the last common factor.

items.skill: Tell a perfect square from a difference of two squares

options.feedback: The two numbers multiply to $9$ and add to $6$, so both are $3$ and the quadratic is a perfect square.
That is $x^{2}-9$, which has no $x$ term. A plus sign in front of the $6x$ means both brackets carry $+3$.
It does. Look for two numbers with product $9$ and sum $6$; $3$ and $3$ work, and they always will when the quadratic is a perfect square.

items.skill: Factorise both lines, then cancel one bracket

options.feedback: Top $\frac{(x+3)(x-3)}{(x+3)^{2}}$, and one $(x+3)$ divides out of each line.
The two $x^{2}$ terms have been struck out, and they are terms of a sum, not factors. Factorise first: the top is $(x+3)(x-3)$ and the bottom is $(x+3)^{2}$.
The bottom is factorised and the top is not, so no common bracket can be seen. Factorise both lines before you look for anything to cancel.

items.skill: Simplify all the way, to a whole number if that is what is left

options.feedback: The bracket $(x+9)$ has gone, but an $x$ still divides both lines. Strike it too and $4$ is left.
Dividing only the top by $4$ changes the fraction's value. Factorise instead: the top is $4x(x+9)$ and the bottom $x(x+9)$, so $4$ is left.

findTheMistake.stem: Erin was asked to simplify fully $\frac{3x^{3}-12x^{2}}{x^{2}-4x}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The bracket was cancelled correctly, and then the working stopped. 3x² over x still has an $x$ on both lines, so it divides again to 3x.

findTheMistake.feedback: Both method-and-working marks for factorising are safe, and the cancelling started correctly. The final mark is for a fraction with nothing left in common, and an $x$ is still a factor of both lines. findTheMistake.stem: Dev was asked to simplify fully $\frac{3x^{2}+27x}{x^{2}+6x-27}$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Dividing only the top by 3 changes the fraction's value. The 3 is a factor of the top, so it has to be taken out and kept: 3x² + 27x = 3x(x + 9).
findTheMistake.feedback: The bottom is factorised correctly, and that mark is safe. The top was divided by 3 before it was factorised, which changes the value, so the answer is a third of the right one. Summer 2019 examiners saw this: candidates who divided by 3 before factorising lost it from the answer. Take a common factor out; never divide it away.
